newsitem.title: JAPAN: Slaying adds to woes of scandal-hit Japan firms.
newsitem.headline: Slaying adds to woes of scandal-hit Japan firms.

text.p: The stabbing death of an executive at Japanese brokerage Yamaichi Securities near his residence has added security fears to the public relations problems facing firms caught in a widening financial scandal, media reports and firms said on Friday.

Police have not linked the slaying on Thursday evening of Koichiro Tarutani, who handled investors' complaints about share transactions, to a racketeer payoff scandal involving Yamaichi and other leading financial firms.
And Yamaichi has said it was "stunned" at the attack but could identify no business-related motive for the slaying, although it still had not clarified all details of the murder.
"Mr Tarutani worked in a section which had no connection whatsoever to the alleged racketeer payoffs and police investigation," said a Yamaichi spokesman.

"It's hard to believe that this was related to business and Mr Tarutani was not known as a personality who had created enemies," the spokesman said, adding that he was not among the firm's executives thought to require protection.

Media reports said that Tarutani's wallet containing about 140,000 yen ($1,196) was left untouched by his murderer, and police are investigating the possibility of the stabbing being motivated by a personal or professional grievance.
Yamaichi, the smallest of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, announced on Monday the resignation of its chairman, president and five vice presidents over suspected payoffs to a racketeer.

The firm is suspected of paying 79 million yen ($675,000) illegally to Ryuichi Koike, the corporate racketeer at the heart of a financial scandal which has also ensnared giant brokerage Nomura Securities and Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB).

More than a dozen people, including top executives from Nomura and DKB, have been arrested in the affair which involved payoffs to "sokaiya" racketeers to stop them from disrupting annual shareholder meetings. Such payments are banned by law.

The saga is unfolding just as Tokyo kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at bringing its financial industry in line with global standards, and has prompted authorities to promise stiffer penalties for future law-breakers.

Business executives have long faulted police for not providing real protection from sokaiya, who are often linked to yakuza crime syndicates and sometimes threaten bodily harm to executives who refuse to pay up.
In one well-publicised case, police blamed a sokaiya for the 1994 murder of a Fuji Photo Film Co official.
Yamaichi executives had been generally advised to keep a low profile while the scandal kept the firm's name in daily headlines, the spokesman said.
A Nomura spokesman declined to comment on the attack or on security policy for its executives, citing safety reasons.
Police said Tarutani, 57, was stabbed numerous times in the stomach and chest in a parking lot near a railway station in Omori, a Tokyo residential area.
Tarutani, whom passersby found drenched in blood and slumped on the ground a 10-minute walk from his home, was rushed to hospital but died shortly after he was admitted.
